<p><code>workLoopConcurrentByScheduler</code> calls <code>shouldYield()</code> after every fiber, asking Scheduler whether the 5 ms are used up. If they are, it leaves the loop and gives the main thread back to the browser. <code>workLoopSync</code> does not ask; it keeps going until <code>workInProgress</code> becomes <code>null</code>.</p>
<h3>Each fiber is visited twice</h3>
<p>Each turn of the loop handles one fiber, in depth-first order. Suppose the component tree is an <code>App</code> with a <code>div</code> under it, and an <code>h1</code> and a <code>p</code> under the <code>div</code>. React visits them in this order:</p>
<ol>
<li><code>beginWork(App)</code></li>
<li><code>beginWork(div)</code></li>
<li><code>beginWork(h1)</code>; <code>h1</code> has no child</li>
<li><code>completeWork(h1)</code>, then move to the sibling</li>
<li><code>beginWork(p)</code>; <code>p</code> has no child</li>
<li><code>completeWork(p)</code>; no more siblings, go back up to the parent</li>
<li><code>completeWork(div)</code></li>
<li><code>completeWork(App)</code></li>
</ol>
<p>On the way down, React calls <code>beginWork</code>: for a function component it runs the function, compares the returned elements with last time, creates or updates the child fibers, and moves to the first child.</p>
<p>On the way up, React calls <code>completeWork</code>: for a host component such as <code>div</code> or <code>span</code>, it creates the DOM node in memory, or records which attributes need to change, then merges its children's flags into its own, so commit knows where in the whole tree something needs to change. A parent's DOM node can only have its children attached once their DOM nodes exist, which is why this happens on the way up.</p>
<p><code>performUnitOfWork</code> itself only calls <code>beginWork</code>. When <code>beginWork</code> returns <code>null</code>, the fiber has no child, so <code>performUnitOfWork</code> calls <code>completeUnitOfWork</code> instead, which runs <code>completeWork</code> and then decides whether to move to the sibling or keep going up.</p>
<h3>Why not recursion</h3>
<p>This walk is a <code>while</code> loop with no recursive calls. Every fiber has the three pointers <code>child</code>, <code>sibling</code>, <code>return</code>, and the loop follows them one step at a time. The current position is kept in the <code>workInProgress</code> variable, not on the JavaScript call stack. So React can stop between any two fibers, give the main thread back to the browser, and continue in the next task from the fiber <code>workInProgress</code> points to.</p>
<p>The reconciler before React 16 walked the component tree recursively, so the current position lived on the call stack. A call stack cannot be saved and resumed later, so the walk had to run to the end in one go. When the React team described Fiber, they called it a "reimplementation of the stack", where each fiber is like a stack frame that can be kept in memory and run again at any time (<a href="https://github.com/acdlite/react-fiber-architecture">React Fiber Architecture</a>).</p>
<p>When the loop ends, the workInProgress tree is built, and every place that needs to change has been marked with a flag.</p>
<h2>4. Output: <code>commitRoot</code></h2>
<p>Once the fiber tree is built, React calls <code>commitRoot</code>.</p>
<p><code>commitRoot</code> runs before mutation, mutation, and layout, in that order, writing the marked changes into the real DOM; <code>useEffect</code> is queued to run later. The green arrow labeled "输出" (output) in the diagram points from <code>commitRoot</code> to <code>react-dom</code>.</p>
<p>These three steps usually finish within one call, and the browser gets no chance to run another task in between. In React 19.3.1, when both of the following hold, the three steps are split into two parts, and the browser runs other tasks between them:</p>
<ul>
<li>The lanes in this commit are only transition, retry, or idle lanes.</li>
<li>This update touches some <code>&#x3C;ViewTransition></code> component. The table below lists the cases that were measured.</li>
</ul>
<p>When both conditions hold, <code>commitRoot</code> finishes before mutation and then calls the browser's <code>document.startViewTransition</code>, putting mutation and layout into its <code>update</code> callback; the browser decides when that runs (<code>commitRoot</code> in <a href="https://github.com/react/react/blob/v19.3.1/packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberWorkLoop.js"><code>ReactFiberWorkLoop.js</code></a>, <code>startViewTransition</code> in <a href="https://github.com/react/react/blob/v19.3.1/packages/react-dom-bindings/src/client/ReactFiberConfigDOM.js"><code>ReactFiberConfigDOM.js</code></a>). An app that uses no <code>&#x3C;ViewTransition></code> always finishes commit within one call.</p>
<details>
<summary>Which updates count as touching a ViewTransition, and the measurements</summary>























































<table><thead><tr><th>Update made inside <code>startTransition</code></th><th>Split into two parts?</th><th>Basis</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>The <code>&#x3C;ViewTransition></code> stays, and the DOM under it changes</td><td>Yes</td><td>Measured</td></tr><tr><td>The <code>&#x3C;ViewTransition></code> stays, and an element under it is removed</td><td>Yes</td><td>Measured</td></tr><tr><td>The <code>&#x3C;ViewTransition></code> itself does not change, and an element next to it, under the same DOM element, is removed</td><td>Yes</td><td>Measured</td></tr><tr><td>A <code>&#x3C;ViewTransition></code> is removed</td><td>Yes</td><td>Measured</td></tr><tr><td>A <code>&#x3C;ViewTransition></code> is added</td><td>Yes</td><td>Measured</td></tr><tr><td>A <code>&#x3C;div></code> is removed, and the <code>&#x3C;ViewTransition></code> is inside that <code>&#x3C;div></code></td><td>No</td><td>Measured</td></tr><tr><td>Same, but the <code>&#x3C;ViewTransition></code> has a <code>name</code>, and the same update adds a <code>&#x3C;ViewTransition></code> with that name elsewhere</td><td>Yes</td><td>Measured</td></tr><tr><td>A <code>&#x3C;div></code> is added, and the <code>&#x3C;ViewTransition></code> is inside that <code>&#x3C;div></code></td><td>No</td><td>Measured</td></tr><tr><td>No <code>&#x3C;ViewTransition></code> on the page</td><td>No</td><td>Measured</td></tr></tbody></table>
<p>"A <code>&#x3C;div></code> is removed, and the <code>&#x3C;ViewTransition></code> is inside that <code>&#x3C;div></code>" does not split. When the <code>&#x3C;div></code> is removed, the whole block disappears with it; React treats a DOM element as one block and does not run a separate exit animation for a <code>&#x3C;ViewTransition></code> inside it (comment in <a href="https://github.com/react/react/blob/v19.3.1/packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberCompleteWork.js"><code>ReactFiberCompleteWork.js</code></a>: "Host Components act as their own View Transitions"). The way it does this: every fiber has a <code>ViewTransitionStatic</code> flag recording "is there a <code>&#x3C;ViewTransition></code> below", and the fiber of a DOM element always clears it. React starts from the removed <code>&#x3C;div></code> and looks down, reads "no", does not go inside, and so does not call <code>document.startViewTransition</code>. Adding a new <code>&#x3C;div></code> follows the same rule: even with a <code>&#x3C;ViewTransition></code> inside the <code>&#x3C;div></code>, the update does not count as touching it.</p>
<p>The next row, with a <code>name</code>, splits again. The same update removes the old <code>&#x3C;ViewTransition name="x"></code> and adds a new <code>&#x3C;ViewTransition name="x"></code> elsewhere on the page. The names match, so React animates the old part of the page into the new position, and it calls <code>document.startViewTransition</code> for that too. React looks under the removed <code>&#x3C;div></code> for a <code>&#x3C;ViewTransition></code> with a <code>name</code>, to pair it with the newly added one. This step reads a different flag, <code>ViewTransitionNamedStatic</code>, which DOM elements do not clear, so a <code>&#x3C;ViewTransition></code> inside the <code>&#x3C;div></code> is still found.</p>
<p>React calls a class component's <code>getSnapshotBeforeUpdate</code> during before mutation and its <code>componentDidUpdate</code> during layout. Measured in Chrome 156 with React 19.3.1: a counter runs alongside, using MessageChannel to keep posting new tasks, and a class component records the counter's value in each of those two methods. The difference between the two values is how many of the counter's own tasks ran in that window; the browser's other tasks are not counted. Three runs per case:</p>






























<table><thead><tr><th>Case</th><th>Called <code>document.startViewTransition</code>?</th><th>Counter tasks run between before mutation and layout</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td><code>setState</code> in a click</td><td>No</td><td>0, 0, 0</td></tr><tr><td><code>startTransition</code></td><td>No</td><td>0, 0, 0</td></tr><tr><td><code>setState</code> in a click, component wrapped in <code>&#x3C;ViewTransition></code></td><td>No</td><td>0, 0, 0</td></tr><tr><td><code>startTransition</code>, component wrapped in <code>&#x3C;ViewTransition></code></td><td>Yes</td><td>5474, 6652, 7124</td></tr></tbody></table>
<p>Only the last case went through View Transition. After before mutation finished, the counter ran five to seven thousand of its tasks before mutation and layout got their turn.</p>
<p>The rows that remove or add an element in the earlier "which updates count" table were measured the same way, three runs each:</p>























































<table><thead><tr><th>Update made inside <code>startTransition</code></th><th>Called <code>document.startViewTransition</code>?</th><th>Counter tasks run between before mutation and layout</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>The <code>&#x3C;ViewTransition></code> stays, an element under it is removed</td><td>Yes</td><td>7218, 6768, 6387</td></tr><tr><td>The <code>&#x3C;ViewTransition></code> itself does not change, an element next to it is removed</td><td>Yes</td><td>6087, 7044, 6998</td></tr><tr><td>A <code>&#x3C;ViewTransition></code> is removed</td><td>Yes</td><td>6494, 6858, 6915</td></tr><tr><td>A <code>&#x3C;div></code> is removed, with the <code>&#x3C;ViewTransition></code> inside</td><td>No</td><td>0, 0, 0</td></tr><tr><td>Same, and a <code>&#x3C;ViewTransition></code> with the same name is added elsewhere</td><td>Yes</td><td>7030, 6847, 6672</td></tr><tr><td>A <code>&#x3C;p></code> is removed, no <code>&#x3C;ViewTransition></code> anywhere</td><td>No</td><td>0, 0, 0</td></tr><tr><td>A <code>&#x3C;ViewTransition></code> is added</td><td>Yes</td><td>5993, 6890, 6712</td></tr><tr><td>A <code>&#x3C;div></code> is added, with the <code>&#x3C;ViewTransition></code> inside</td><td>No</td><td>0, 0, 0</td></tr><tr><td>A <code>&#x3C;p></code> is added, no <code>&#x3C;ViewTransition></code> anywhere</td><td>No</td><td>0, 0, 0</td></tr></tbody></table>
<p>The same nine updates made in a click's <code>setState</code> never called <code>document.startViewTransition</code>, and the counter difference was 0 every time.</p>
</details>
<p>The reconciler itself never touches the DOM. Functions it calls, such as <code>appendChild</code>, <code>insertBefore</code>, <code>removeChild</code>, <code>commitUpdate</code>, are implemented by react-dom (<a href="https://github.com/react/react/blob/v19.3.1/packages/react-dom-bindings/src/client/ReactFiberConfigDOM.js"><code>ReactFiberConfigDOM.js</code></a>), and those are what call the DOM APIs. After this step the DOM has changed, and it is the browser's turn to run Style Recalc, Layout, Paint, and Composite.</p>
<h2>The four steps at a glance</h2>



































<table><thead><tr><th>Step</th><th>Function in React 19.3.1</th><th>What it does</th><th>Can it stop halfway?</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>1. Input</td><td><code>scheduleUpdateOnFiber</code></td><td>Pick the lane, record the update on the fiber and the root</td><td>No render yet; finishes on the spot</td></tr><tr><td>2. Register</td><td><code>ensureRootIsScheduled</code>, then <code>scheduleTaskForRootDuringMicrotask</code> in the microtask</td><td><code>SyncLane</code> stays in the microtask; other lanes go to Scheduler</td><td>No render yet; finishes on the spot</td></tr><tr><td>3. Build the fiber tree</td><td><code>performUnitOfWork</code> (<code>beginWork</code>, <code>completeWork</code>)</td><td>Build workInProgress, compare with last time, create DOM nodes</td><td>Only for transition, retry, idle lanes</td></tr><tr><td>4. Output</td><td><code>commitRoot</code></td><td>Write the changes into the DOM</td><td>Usually not; when a transition touches a <code>&#x3C;ViewTransition></code>, other tasks run between before mutation and mutation</td></tr></tbody></table>
<h2>Most components do not run again</h2>
<p>Every update walks from the root, and after an interruption it starts again from the root, which sounds expensive. But most fibers <strong>bail out</strong>, meaning React does not run that component again.</p>
<p>When <code>beginWork</code> reaches a fiber whose props are the same object as last time, with no context change and no pending update of its own, React does not run that component again, and then looks below it:</p>
<ul>
<li>Nothing below has a pending update either: the whole subtree is skipped, and no component inside it runs.</li>
<li>Some descendant has an update: this component does not run, but React keeps walking down until it reaches that descendant.</li>
</ul>
<p>Each fiber's <code>childLanes</code> records whether anything below it has a pending update, so even though React starts from the root, it only walks into the paths that changed.</p>
<p>Measured in Chrome 156, same result on React 18.3.1 and 19.3.1, three runs each. <code>Parent</code> has three children: <code>Plain</code>, not wrapped in memo; <code>Memo</code>, wrapped in <code>React.memo</code>, with <code>Inner</code> under it; and <code>MemoOuter</code>, also wrapped in memo, with <code>Middle</code> under it and <code>Leaf</code>, which has its own state, under that:</p>

















<table><thead><tr><th>Whose state changed</th><th>Components that rendered again</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td><code>Parent</code></td><td><code>Parent</code>, <code>Plain</code></td></tr><tr><td><code>Leaf</code></td><td><code>Leaf</code></td></tr></tbody></table>
<p>When <code>Parent</code> updated, neither <code>Memo</code> nor <code>Inner</code> ran. When <code>Leaf</code> updated, <code>Parent</code>, <code>MemoOuter</code>, and <code>Middle</code> did not run; React followed <code>childLanes</code> down to <code>Leaf</code>.</p>
<p>You can make more fibers skip. <code>React.memo</code> lets a child skip when its parent runs again, as long as every prop is the same as last time; <code>useMemo</code> and <code>useCallback</code> keep the objects and functions you pass down the same between renders, so that comparison passes.</p>
<p>When <code>setState</code> receives the same value as the current one (compared with <code>Object.is</code>), React usually drops the update before scheduling anything, but not every time. The React docs also say "in some cases React may still need to call your component before skipping the children" (<a href="https://react.dev/reference/react/useState">useState</a>). Measured results, same on React 18.3.1 and 19.3.1, three runs each:</p>


























<table><thead><tr><th>Case</th><th>Click 1</th><th>Click 2</th><th>Click 3</th><th>Click 4</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>state is 0, every click calls <code>setN(0)</code></td><td>nothing renders</td><td>nothing renders</td><td>nothing renders</td><td>nothing renders</td></tr><tr><td>state is 0, every click calls <code>setN(1)</code></td><td><code>App</code>, <code>Child</code></td><td><code>App</code></td><td>nothing renders</td><td>nothing renders</td></tr></tbody></table>
<p>In the second case, on click 2 the value is already 1, yet <code>App</code> still rendered once, while <code>Child</code> under it was skipped. <code>dispatchSetState</code> compares the old and new values before scheduling, and drops the update if they are equal, only when neither this fiber nor its alternate has a pending lane.</p>
<details>
<summary>Why click 2 still renders: lanes on the two fibers</summary>
<p>When <code>App</code> first mounts, React creates only one fiber; its <code>alternate</code> is <code>null</code>, and the second copy is not created until the first update. So on click 1, <code>setState</code> records <code>SyncLane</code> on that one fiber only. During the render, React copies a second fiber from it and clears the second fiber's <code>lanes</code> to 0 before running <code>App</code>. After commit, the second fiber becomes the one on screen and the first becomes the alternate. This render cleared only the second fiber's <code>lanes</code>; the first still carries <code>SyncLane</code>.</p>
<p>Reading the <code>lanes</code> of <code>App</code>'s two fibers before each click, three runs each on React 18.3.1 and 19.3.1, all identical:</p>




















<table><thead><tr><th>When read</th><th><code>lanes</code> of the fiber on screen</th><th><code>lanes</code> of the alternate</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Before click 2</td><td>0</td><td><code>SyncLane</code> (1 in 18.3.1, 2 in 19.3.1)</td></tr><tr><td>Before click 3</td><td>0</td><td>0</td></tr></tbody></table>
<p>So on click 2, <code>dispatchSetState</code> did not compare the values; it recorded <code>SyncLane</code> on both fibers and scheduled a render. This render uses the alternate, and React clears its <code>lanes</code> to 0 before running <code>App</code>. <code>App</code> computes the same state as last time, so React calls <code>bailoutHooks</code> (<a href="https://github.com/react/react/blob/v19.3.1/packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberHooks.js"><code>ReactFiberHooks.js</code></a>), which removes <code>SyncLane</code> from the fiber on screen too, and then skips <code>Child</code>. Only at this point are both fibers' <code>lanes</code> 0. On click 3 both are 0, so <code>dispatchSetState</code> compares the values, finds them equal, and drops the update.</p>
</details>
<h2>Three packages, one job each</h2>
<p>The diagram separates three things that often get mixed together:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Scheduler</strong> decides when to run.</li>
<li><strong>The reconciler</strong> (ReactFiberWorkLoop in the diagram) decides how to build the fiber tree and what needs to change.</li>
<li><strong>react-dom</strong> writes those changes into the DOM.</li>
</ul>
<p><code>scheduler</code> is a dependency of react-dom and is installed along with it. The reconciler's code, on the other hand, is compiled straight into react-dom: <code>react-dom-client.production.js</code> in react-dom 19.3.1 defines <code>beginWork</code> and <code>performUnitOfWork</code> itself, and the only things it <code>require</code>s are <code>react</code>, <code>react-dom</code>, and <code>scheduler</code>.</p>
<p><code>react-reconciler</code> is also published as its own npm package for people writing their own renderer. ink 8.0.0 lists it as a dependency, and react-three-fiber 9.8.2 ships a bundled copy of react-reconciler inside its own package. React Native's renderer is compiled from the same reconciler source too. Swap out react-dom, and the same reconciler can draw components into a 3D scene (react-three-fiber) or a terminal (ink).</p>
<p><img src="https://7km.top/static/core-packages.c2850581.png" alt="React core packages">
<em>How the three core packages, react-dom, react-reconciler and scheduler, call each other (React 17.0.2). Credit: <a href="https://7km.top/main/macro-structure">7km.top macro package structure</a>.</em></p>
<h2>How the APIs you use connect to the four steps</h2>
<p>Most of these four steps happen in places you never import. Compared with the packages you do touch:</p>






























<table><thead><tr><th>Package</th><th>Do you import it?</th><th>Role</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td><code>react</code></td><td>yes, every day</td><td>the component API: <code>useState</code>, <code>useMemo</code>, <code>startTransition</code></td></tr><tr><td><code>react-dom</code></td><td>yes</td><td>the entry point and DOM output: <code>createRoot</code>, <code>flushSync</code>; the reconciler is compiled in here too</td></tr><tr><td><code>react-reconciler</code></td><td>no</td><td>the reconciler, used only when writing your own renderer</td></tr><tr><td><code>scheduler</code></td><td>no</td><td>when that work runs, and for how long at a time</td></tr></tbody></table>
<p><code>startTransition</code> sends the render through <code>renderRootConcurrent</code>, which pauses every 5 ms, so one long transition render does not freeze the tab; a long render triggered by a click or <code>setTimeout</code> goes through <code>renderRootSync</code> and still freezes it. <code>React.memo</code> lets <code>beginWork</code> in step 3 skip that component.</p>
<h2>Environment</h2>
